Report each category’s HR@10 and the equally weighted four-category macro mean, plus paired absolute differences in percentage points. Adapting [Smucker et al.’s retrieval comparison methods](https://ciir-publications.cs.umass.edu/getpdf.php?id=744), bootstrap users within each category: sample 200 user indices with replacement, preserve both models’ outcomes and fixed candidate sets together, then average the four category differences. Use, for example, 10,000 replicates and a 95% percentile interval. Report discordant hit counts as well. These intervals describe user-sampling uncertainty conditional on trained models and pinned candidates; they exclude training-seed, negative-sampling, and new-category variability. For the exact fixed benchmark users, observed differences are descriptive quantities.

Repeated checkpoint and hyperparameter selection can overfit validation noise: [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) show selection bias can rival algorithm differences. Disclose configurations tried, checkpoints inspected, selection frequency, stopping rule, and the complete search trajectory. A bootstrap interval computed after choosing the winner does not remove selection optimism. Keep seed 42 and the evaluator unchanged; label search comparisons exploratory and reserve confirmatory claims for the host’s untouched final evaluation. Ordinary multiple-comparison adjustments alone do not resolve adaptive validation reuse.

Label results explicitly as HR@10 against 99 unique sampled negatives, evaluation seed 42. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) show sampled ranking metrics can reverse full-catalog model ordering even in expectation. Therefore, narrow paired intervals establish neither full-catalog superiority nor recommendation quality for the twenty simulator users. Preserve the pinned metric for selection, state this limitation, and distinguish any permitted full-catalog qualitative diagnostics from benchmark evidence.
